morph.note: समाध्मात is the past participle of सम् + आ + √ध्मा (‘to blow’, as into a conch or bellows): ‘inflated’.
Present participle of आ + √पत्, ‘flying at, rushing upon’; accusative because it describes the object of दृष्ट्वा.
Dative of purpose (तादर्थ्य): ‘for the sake of his killing’.

mantras.anvaya: इति क्रोधसमाध्मातम् आपतन्तं महासुरं दृष्ट्वा सा चण्डिका तदा तद्वधाय कोपम् अकरोत्।
mantras.lit: Seeing the great asura thus swollen with rage and rushing upon (her), Caṇḍikā then made (her) anger for his slaying.
mantras.tr: Seeing the great demon bearing down on her, bursting with rage, Caṇḍikā then turned her wrath to his destruction.
mantras.tr_note: कोपम् अकरोत् ‘made anger’ is rendered ‘turned her wrath’; तद्वधाय gives its aim.

comm.t: A turning point. Her anger in 3.24 was at the attack on her lion; now it is directed (तद्वधाय) at his death. From 3.29 on she acts against Mahiṣa alone.

Caṇḍikā, the name the narrator uses here and in 3.34–35, is also a name of the Goddess in the Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa), name 755, चण्डिका. The two texts share the name; the battle here belongs to the Devī Māhātmya alone.

samasa.vigraha: महत् च तत् मृधं च, तस्मिन्
samasa.sense: in the thick of the great battle

morph.note: Perfect of √बन्ध्: reduplicated ब-, root unchanged in the singular. The past participle बद्ध (बन्ध् + त → बद्ध: the nasal is lost, and dh + t gives ddh) follows in the second line.
Perfect of √त्यज्: reduplication त-, vṛddhi of the root a in the third singular.

The genitive marks the person towards whom the noose is thrown; a locative or dative would be the stricter construction. It cannot mean ‘his noose’: the noose is the Goddess’s, the gift of the lord of waters (पाशं चाम्बुपतिर्ददौ, 2.23).

mantras.anvaya: सा तस्य (उपरि) पाशं क्षिप्त्वा वै तं महासुरं बबन्ध। महामृधे बद्धः सः अपि माहिषं रूपं तत्याज।
mantras.anvaya_en: Two sentences: the binding (absolutive + perfect) and his response, with बद्धः as a participle of circumstance.
mantras.lit: She, having cast the noose upon him, indeed bound that great asura. He too, bound in the great battle, gave up (his) buffalo form.
mantras.tr: She cast her noose over him and bound the great demon. Caught fast in the great battle, he shed his buffalo form.

comm.t: The noose — Varuṇa’s gift (2.23) — holds the buffalo, and the asura escapes it by escaping his body: the shape-changing of 3.29–33 begins. Each new form is a way out of what has caught the last one.
A modern reading: what is bound in one form slips away into another. The pursuit through lion, man and elephant shows a problem that keeps changing its shape until it is met at its root.

sandhi.note: -aḥ + a- → -o ’-; the t of अभवत् stays unvoiced before s, and सद्यः before the voiced y becomes सद्यो (हशि च, 6.1.114).
t before t stays t; a + a → ā.
After i the visarga (as ru) appears as r before a vowel.

samasa.literal: he in whose hand is a sword
samasa.alt: A bahuvrīhi of the ‘weapon-in-hand’ type, in which the thing held stands first (cf. चक्रपाणि, शूलपाणि).

morph.note: Present of √छिद् with the nasal infix of the rudhādi class (छि-न-त्-ति; d → t before t). After यावत् the present is used for an action on the point of happening: ‘while Ambikā is (about to) cut off his head’.

mantras.anvaya: ततः (सः) सद्यः सिंहः अभवत्। यावत् अम्बिका तस्य शिरः छिनत्ति, तावत् खड्गपाणिः पुरुषः अदृश्यत।
mantras.anvaya_en: A statement, then a correlative time clause (यावत् … तावत्): ‘just as … at that very moment …’.
mantras.lit: Then at once he became a lion. Just as Ambikā is cutting off his head, at that moment a man, sword in hand, was seen.
mantras.tr: At once he became a lion. But just as Ambikā was about to cut off its head, a man appeared, sword in hand.
mantras.tr_note: The Sanskrit present after यावत् is rendered by the English past of intention (‘was about to’).

comm.t: Two changes in one verse: buffalo to lion, lion to armed man. The यावत् … तावत् construction makes the escape exact — the new form appears at the very instant of the blow.

samasa.vigraha: खड्गश्च चर्म च, तयोः समाहारः खड्गचर्म, तेन
samasa.sense: with his sword and his shield
samasa.alt: As an itaretara dvandva it would be dual (खड्गचर्मभ्याम्). The neuter singular shows a samāhāra: pairs of arms and parts of an army are commonly collected into one unit this way.

morph.note: Perfect of √छिद्: reduplicated चि- (छ् → च्), the cch written double between vowels, guṇa of i in the singular (छेद).
Instrumental singular of the neuter n-stem चर्मन् ‘shield, hide’ as the last member: -चर्मणा (n → ṇ after r).
Root aorist of √भू; as in 1.4, a narrative past alongside the perfect and imperfect.

mantras.anvaya: ततः एव आशु देवी तं पुरुषं खड्गचर्मणा सार्धं सायकैः चिच्छेद। ततः सः महागजः अभूत्।
mantras.anvaya_en: पुरुषम् and तम् refer to the same man: the second line resumes him with the pronoun so that ‘with his sword and shield’ can be added.
mantras.lit: Right then the Goddess swiftly cut down the man with arrows — him together with (his) sword and shield. Then he became a great elephant.
mantras.tr: At that very moment the Goddess cut the man down with her arrows, sword, shield and all. Then he turned into a huge elephant.

comm.t: The man is cut down with the very arms he appeared with (3.30), and the asura escapes again, now as an elephant: buffalo, lion, man, elephant.

sandhi.note: Final m → anusvāra before a consonant (also करं देवी).
The prefix निस् shows r before the vowel of the augment.

morph.note: Present participle कर्षत् (√कृष् + शतृ), genitive singular: ‘the trunk of (him) dragging’ — the participle describes the elephant in the act.

√कृत् (कृन्तति, with the nasal of the मुचादि group) is a parasmaipada root, whose imperfect is अकृन्तत्. The printed form has the ātmanepada ending -त: a Purāṇic (ārṣa) use of the middle for the active, of a kind common in epic Sanskrit. It is not a passive (that would be अकृत्यत).
Perfect of √कृष्: reduplication च- (क् → च्), guṇa ṛ → ar in the singular.

mantras.anvaya: (सः महागजः) करेण तं महासिंहं चकर्ष जगर्ज च। देवी तु कर्षतः (तस्य) करं खड्गेन निरकृन्तत।
mantras.anvaya_en: The elephant is the subject of the first line (from 3.31); the second turns to the Goddess with तु.
mantras.lit: And with (his) trunk he dragged that great lion and trumpeted. But the Goddess cut off with (her) sword the trunk of (him) dragging.
mantras.tr: With his trunk he dragged at the great lion, trumpeting; but as he dragged, the Goddess cut off his trunk with her sword.

comm.t: As in 3.24, the asura goes for the lion, and again the Goddess answers for it. The elephant’s weapon, its trunk, is cut off in the act of using it.
